```{r}
data = read.csv("Admissions.csv") 
head(data)
```

# b)

```{r}
tab.a <- xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit + Dept, data = data)
tab.a
```

```{r}
# Conditional independence Gender/Admission
model.a.1 <- glm(Freq ~ Gender + Admit + Dept + Gender:Dept + Admit:Dept,
          family = poisson, data = data)

# Homogeneous association adding Gender:Admit
model.a.2 <- glm(Freq ~ Gender + Admit + Dept + Gender:Admit + Gender:Dept + Admit:Dept,
          family = poisson, data = data)

# Test: is Gender:Admit needed? model.a.1 compared model.a.2
anova(model.a.1, model.a.2, test = "Chisq")
```
## Conclusion:

Fail to reject H0. Adding Gender:Admit does not significantly improve fit, conditional independence holds. Within each department, gender has no additional effect on admission beyond what is already captured by Gender:Dept and Admit:Dept.

# b)

```{r}
# Separate admitted and rejected
admitted <- data[data$Admit == "Admitted", c("Gender", "Dept", "Freq")]
rejected  <- data[data$Admit == "Rejected", c("Gender", "Dept", "Freq")]

# Merge by Gender and Dept
new_data <- merge(admitted, rejected, by = c("Gender", "Dept"))
names(new_data)[3:4] <- c("Admitted", "Rejected")
head(new_data)
```
```{r}
# Fit the model
model.b <- glm(cbind(Admitted, Rejected) ~ Gender + Dept,
               family = "binomial",
               data = new_data)
summ.b = summary(model.b)
summ.b
```
The **regression parameters** represent the log-odds ratio relative to the reference group (Female, Dept A).

## Summary

The fitted model regresses the probability of admission on Gender and Department using a logistic link. The reference category is Female applicants in Department A.

**Intercept (0.682, p < 0.001):** The baseline log-odds of admission for a Female in Dept A is 0.682, corresponding to an admission probability of approximately 66%, the highest admission rate across all groups.

**GenderMale (−0.100, p = 0.217):** The Wald test is non-significant. There is no evidence that gender affects admission probability once department is accounted for. This confirms the conditional independence finding from the log-linear analysis.

**Department effects:** All departments show lower admission odds than Dept A, with effects growing progressively stronger from B through F. Only Dept B is non-significant (p = 0.693), meaning it has a similar admission rate to Dept A. Depts C, D, E, and F are all highly significant (p < 2e-16), with odds ratios of 0.283, 0.274, 0.175, and 0.037 respectively. Dept F is the most selective by far, applicants there have only about 4% of the admission odds of a Dept A applicant.

**Conclusion:** The Wald tests paint a clear picture, admission outcomes are almost entirely determined by department, not gender. The apparent gender gap observed marginally disappears once department is controlled suggesting a Simpson's paradox.

# c)

```{r}
# Fitted from binomial
p_hat  <- fitted(model.b)
total  <- new_data$Admitted + new_data$Rejected
fitted_admitted_binom <- p_hat * total
fitted_rejected_binom <- (1 - p_hat) * total

# Fitted from log-linear
loglin_fitted <- data.frame(
  Gender  = data$Gender,
  Dept    = data$Dept,
  Admit   = data$Admit,
  Fitted  = fitted(model.a.2)
)

admitted_loglin <- loglin_fitted[loglin_fitted$Admit == "Admitted", ]
rejected_loglin <- loglin_fitted[loglin_fitted$Admit == "Rejected", ]

# Merge to align with new_data order
admitted_loglin <- merge(new_data[, c("Gender","Dept")], admitted_loglin, 
                         by = c("Gender","Dept"))
rejected_loglin <- merge(new_data[, c("Gender","Dept")], rejected_loglin, 
                         by = c("Gender","Dept"))

# Final comparison
result <- data.frame(
  Gender          = new_data$Gender,
  Dept            = new_data$Dept,
  binom_admitted  = round(fitted_admitted_binom, 4),
  loglin_admitted = round(admitted_loglin$Fitted, 4),
  binom_rejected  = round(fitted_rejected_binom, 4),
  loglin_rejected = round(rejected_loglin$Fitted, 4)
)

result
```
We exactly have the same fitted counts for the binomial (b) compared to log-linear (poisson).

# d)

```{r}
# Fitted probabilities
new_data$p_hat <- fitted(model.b)

# Compute odds for each row
new_data$odds <- new_data$p_hat / (1 - new_data$p_hat)

# Separate female and male
odds_female <- new_data[new_data$Gender == "Female", c("Dept", "odds")]
odds_male   <- new_data[new_data$Gender == "Male",   c("Dept", "odds")]

# Merge and compute ratio Female/Male
odds_ratio <- merge(odds_female, odds_male, by = "Dept")
names(odds_ratio)[2:3] <- c("odds_female", "odds_male")
odds_ratio$ratio_F_over_M <- odds_ratio$odds_female / odds_ratio$odds_male

odds_ratio
```

# e)

```{r}
# Get fitted values from conditional independence model (model.a.1)
loglin_fitted <- data.frame(
  Gender = data$Gender,
  Dept   = data$Dept,
  Admit  = data$Admit,
  Fitted = fitted(model.a.1)
)

# Separate admitted and rejected
admitted <- loglin_fitted[loglin_fitted$Admit == "Admitted", ]
rejected  <- loglin_fitted[loglin_fitted$Admit == "Rejected", ]

# Compute odds = admitted/rejected for each Gender x Dept
merged <- merge(admitted, rejected, by = c("Gender", "Dept"))
merged$odds <- merged$Fitted.x / merged$Fitted.y

# Separate female and male
odds_female <- merged[merged$Gender == "Female", c("Dept", "odds")]
odds_male   <- merged[merged$Gender == "Male",   c("Dept", "odds")]

# Merge and compute ratio Female/Male
odds_ratio <- merge(odds_female, odds_male, by = "Dept")
names(odds_ratio)[2:3] <- c("odds_female", "odds_male")
odds_ratio$ratio_F_over_M <- odds_ratio$odds_female / odds_ratio$odds_male

print(odds_ratio)
```

The conditional independence model (model.a.1) gives odds ratios of exactly 1 in every department, gender and admission are completely unrelated within departments by construction, since there is no Gender:Admit term.

The binomial model (model.b) gives a constant ratio of 1.105 across departments, slightly favouring females.

 Both are constant across departments, confirming the main effects structure in both cases.
